questions.question: List the names and formulae of the four required acids and five required bases, and give one everyday or industrial identity for each acid.
questions.expected_answer: The acids: hydrochloric acid, HCl — stomach acid and diluted pool acid; nitric acid, HNO₃ — the acid of fertiliser manufacture; sulphuric acid, H₂SO₄ — car battery acid and the most-produced industrial chemical; ethanoic (acetic) acid, CH₃COOH — the acid of vinegar. The bases: sodium hydroxide, NaOH (caustic soda, in drain cleaner); potassium hydroxide, KOH; ammonia, NH₃ (the sharp smell in some household cleaners); sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃ (washing soda); and sodium hydrogen carbonate, NaHCO₃ (baking soda or bicarbonate of soda).

questions.question: Using ionic charges, explain why sulphuric acid is H₂SO₄ while hydrochloric acid is HCl, and why sodium carbonate is Na₂CO₃ while sodium hydrogen carbonate is NaHCO₃. Then explain why ethanoic acid is monoprotic despite showing four hydrogens in its formula.
questions.expected_answer: Charges in a formula must total zero. Chloride is Cl⁻ with a single minus, so one H⁺ balances it: HCl. Sulphate is SO₄²⁻, whose double negative needs two H⁺ ions: H₂SO₄. Carbonate is CO₃²⁻ and requires two Na⁺ ions: Na₂CO₃. Hydrogen carbonate, HCO₃⁻, has already gained a hydrogen that cancels one of the two negative charges, so its remaining single minus takes just one Na⁺: NaHCO₃. Ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH, is monoprotic because only the final hydrogen, bonded to oxygen, is acidic; the three hydrogens of the CH₃ group are bonded to carbon and are never released in water. It is additionally a weak acid, releasing even that one hydrogen reluctantly and incompletely — which is why vinegar is safe to eat.

questions.question: State the general products of neutralisation and the rule linking a salt's name to its parents. Then choose an acid and a base to prepare sodium sulphate, and write the balanced equation for potassium hydroxide neutralising sulphuric acid.
questions.expected_answer: Acid plus base gives a salt plus water. The salt's first name — its metal — comes from the base; its surname comes from the acid: hydrochloric acid fathers chlorides, nitric acid nitrates, sulphuric acid sulphates, and ethanoic acid ethanoates. To prepare sodium sulphate, read the name apart: sodium from sodium hydroxide, sulphate from sulphuric acid — so use NaOH and H₂SO₄. For potassium hydroxide and sulphuric acid: 2KOH + H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O — two potassium hydroxide per acid, because the diprotic acid carries two hydrogens needing two hydroxides, giving potassium sulphate and two water molecules.
